blocks.text: But the Hebrew has הגה, which is rightly rendered by the verb to moan, since it everywhere refers to mourning. So in the song of King Hezekiah about his illness, Es. XXXVIII,14. [II, 540] אהגה כיונה, I moaned like a dove. And Es. LIX, 11., where the afflicted condition of the Jews is treated: We all growl like bears, וכיונים הגה נהגה, and like doves we moan with moaning, that is, with heavy and continuous moaning ^{(4)}. But המה too, which properly means to roar, applies to the moaning of doves, when it is said in Ezech. VII, 16. כיוני הגאות כלם הומות איש בעונו, like doves of the valleys they all roared (that is, moaned), each for his own sin. For כיוני הגיאות, like doves of the valleys, the Septuagint read כיונה הגות. Hence arose that rendering ὡς περιστεραὶ μελετητικαὶ [hōs peristerai meletētikai], like moaning doves. For with them μελετᾷν [meletan], said of doves, means to moan. Accordingly Theodoret on this passage: Ὀδυρόμενοι γὰρ καὶ θρηνοῦντες περιστεραῖς μελετώσαις ἀπεικαθήσονται· στένουσι γὰρ ἔοικε τῶν περιστερῶν ἡ φωνή [Odyromenoi gar kai thrēnountes peristerais meletōsais apeikasthēsontai; stenousi gar eoike tōn peristerōn hē phōnē]. This must certainly be rendered thus: For those who lament and mourn will be compared to moaning doves (not to doves on high, as the translator has it here). For the voice of doves is like that of people moaning. The voice of the dove is also taken for mournful moaning in Nahum II, 7., where the queen of Nineveh, as she is led into captivity, is accompanied by maidservants moaning, as with the voice of doves, and beating their breasts. The Hebrew has מנהגות כקול יונים, leading away as with the voice of doves. Leading away here, as they hold, is the same as accompanying, and moaning must be supplied. For to lead away is put for to lead away and to moan: one for two. So in Prov. XXV, 22., You will take coals of fire upon his head, for you will take and put; and Psal. LXVIII, 19., You received gifts for men, for you received and gave, or you received things to give. Accordingly Paul renders it he gave gifts to men, Ephes. IV, 8. What if for מנהגות, leading away, one were to read מהגות, moaning, with one small letter less? The sense would thus be plainer; yet I would not dare to change anything, since it is established that the most ancient translators read מנהגות ^{(5)}.

Scripture praises the flight of the dove more than once. Thus Esa. LX, 8.: Who are these that fly together like clouds, and like doves to their windows? The Rabbis refer this [II, 541] to the Israelites, who were to return from the Babylonian captivity with the greatest eagerness. Hence the Chaldee paraphrast: Who are these who come openly like swift clouds without delay? The exiles of Israel, who are gathered and return to their land, כיונין דתיבין לגו שובכיהן, like doves that return to their dovecotes. On these words Kimchi: יותר יעופו מהרה בשובם אל קניהם ממה שיעופו בצאתם מהם מפני שהם ממהרות לשוב אל גוזליהם שהניחו להאכילם מאשר בפיהם, They fly faster when they return to their nests than when they go out from them, because they hasten to return to the young they have left, to offer them the food which they have in their mouth. A similar passage is Os. XI, 11.: They will tremble like a little bird out of Egypt, and like a dove from the land of Assyria. They will tremble, יחרדו, that is, they will hurry up in agitation. So 1 Sam. XVI, 4., when Samuel came to Bethlehem, ויחרדו, And the elders of the city trembled (that is, hurried in agitation) to meet him. And in this same prophet, Ose. III, 5.: They will tremble to the Lord and to his goodness, that is, they will hurry up in agitation. Aben Ezra: [col. 14] ישובו במהרה במרוצא פתע פתאום, They will return hastily, at a run, quickly, swiftly. Yet in the sacred text there is not חרדו but its synonym פחדו. Indeed, verbs of trembling sometimes relate to haste. Virgil, in the ninth book of the Aeneid:
Do not tremble, Teucrians, to defend my ships.

that is, do not hurry. So Servius and Nonius Marcellus. And Livy, book 23: And soon, while each hurries [trepidat] running about to his own duties at the first signals. Trepidat, that is, festinat [hurries]. So certainly in Hosea: They will tremble like a dove (that is, they will flee with the utmost haste) from Assyria ^{(6)}. For the flight of the dove is extremely swift. Hence it is that in Psal. LV, 7. David wishes for the wings of a dove, to withdraw by swift flight from imminent danger. Who (he says) will give me a wing like a dove's, with which I might fly away to safety? Behold, I would wander as far away as possible, to stay in the wilderness. And I would hasten my escape, swifter than the most rapid wind and whirlwind. Just as the Chorus in Sophocles' Oedipus at Colonus:

Εἴτ᾽, ἀελλαία ταχύῤ- [Eit', aellaia tachyr-] Would that, like a dove of swift ῥωστος πελειὰς, [rhōstos peleias,] whirlwind onrush, Αἰθερίας νεφέλας [Aitherias nephelas] I might pass through Κύρσαί με, [Kyrsai me,] etc. the ethereal clouds, etc.
